narrative.text: Fig. 1, 'From paper to digital: a transformational journey'. The upper half is a rising staircase of four stages, each an icon and a heading — PAPER, DIGITIZATION, DIGITALIZATION, DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION — joined by arrows labelled 'From paper to digital', 'Improve existing processes' and 'Fundamentally change healthcare delivery'. A vertical axis, 'Data use', runs from 'Limited data use with little to no interoperability standards adopted' at the bottom to 'Greater data use with greater adoption of interoperability standards' at the top; a horizontal arrow beneath is labelled 'Process Optimization'. The lower half is a table with one column per stage (Paper, Digitization, Digitalization, Digital transformation) and five rows: Definition, Examples, Benefits, Challenges and Dependencies. For example, Paper is defined as manually capturing and processing data in paper formats, with examples such as paper register books and tally sheets; Digital transformation is defined as digitally optimizing and driving systems-level change through innovation, analytics and feedback mechanisms, with examples such as algorithms for personalized treatment plans.

narrative.text: Fig. 3, 'Delivering an integrated ecosystem of information systems and digital health solutions supports the PHC approach'. Four nested layers surround a figure labelled 'Centered around the needs of the care seeker'. From innermost to outermost: COMMUNITY LINKAGES AND ENGAGEMENT (community health workers, care seekers) holds patient portal, targeted messaging, CHW job aid, self-monitoring devices and capacity building; ORGANIZATION AND MANAGEMENT (primary care providers) holds clinical job aids, AI risk assessment, referral and coordination, and an electronic health record; SELECTION, DESIGN AND PLANNING OF SERVICES (health system decision makers) holds a dashboard and management information systems; DEFINING A TARGET POPULATION AND UNDERSTANDING THEIR NEEDS (policy makers) holds civil registration and vital statistics, and disease surveillance. Each solution carries a one-line purpose. A note says solutions can span more than one layer and are allocated to one only for illustration.

basis.saw: Fig. 4, a five-tier stack of data uses with a person at the base

narrative.text: Fig. 4, 'The added value of “collect once, use for many purposes” principle'. Five stacked tiers rise from a person icon at the base. Bottom to top: Primary, individual data collection (clinical, lab, pharmacy, registries and ID data); Person-centred health service delivery (clinical decision support, scheduling, case management); Programme management (operational decision support, quality improvement, facility management, process optimization); Health system monitoring (national strategic plans and policies, national indicators, accountability); and Global monitoring (accountability towards the SDGs). A side bar groups the lower two tiers as 'Primary data use' and the upper three as 'Secondary data use'.

basis.saw: Fig. 5, five knowledge layers L1–L5 flowing through localisation to country adaptation

narrative.text: Fig. 5, 'WHO SMART Guidelines approach'. A 'Research and evidence base' bar feeds five knowledge layers, each with its product: L1 Narrative (enhanced guidelines), L2 Operational (digital adaptation kits), L3 Machine readable (machine-readable recommendations), L4 Executable (reference software) and L5 Dynamic (precision health models). Each layer passes through a 'Localisation' bar into a matching country-implementation adaptation: national policies and guidelines (L1), localised requirements (L2), localised machine-readable code and standards (L3), localised static digital services (L4) and dynamic digital applications optimised for local outcomes (L5). All five feed 'Data, evidence, and impact', which loops back to the evidence base as 'Evidence from digital implementations'.

narrative.text: Fig. 6, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven numbered phases run down the left: 01 Assessing the current state and enabling environment; 02 Establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; 03 Defining the future state; 04 Planning the enterprise architecture; 05 Determining health content requirements; 06 M&E of digital health implementations and fostering data use; 07 Implementing, maintaining and scaling. Each phase lists its steps, for example 'Develop a national digital health strategy' in phase 02 and 'Identify validated health content appropriate for the implementation context' in phase 05. To the right, resource tiles are placed against the phase(s) they serve, some spanning several phases, and each is marked as a PDF for print or an online environment. They include the WHO–ITU national eHealth strategy toolkit, the Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG), the WHO SMART guidelines with digital adaptation kits and machine-readable recommendations, TOGAF, Open HIE, ICD-11, HL7 FHIR, LOINC, the WHO MAPS toolkit and Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health. The tile 'WHO handbook for digitalizing primary health care (this document)' sits in phase 05.

narrative.text: Fig. 7, 'Iterative and agile approach'. Three circular loops sit along a horizontal timeline arrow: Minimum viable product (MVP), then VERSION 1, then VERSION 2. Each loop has the same four stages: understand and prioritize user requirements, design (adapt design in later versions), build and test, and train users. Milestones along the arrow read: determine that a PCPOSS is an appropriate health intervention; repeat the previous loop until meeting MVP specs to deploy; deploy and roll out; gather and manage user feedback; deploy and roll out; gather and manage user feedback; deploy, roll out and scale; and iterations for continuous improvement.

narrative.text: Fig. 9, 'Example business process matrix from family planning DAK'. A table with the columns Process name, Process ID, Personas, Objectives and Task set, the header row defining each column. Three processes follow. A Registration (FP.A), with client and clerk or health-care provider, ensures the client is in the system and queued for counselling; its tasks are to search for, review and update, or create a client record. B Family planning counselling (FP.B), with client and health-care provider, discusses methods and selects one the client is medically eligible for; its tasks run from taking a history and a risk assessment through checking medical eligibility criteria and stock to referral if the facility cannot provide the method. C Service provision (FP.C) provides the chosen method, covering informed consent, start timing, dual protection and follow-up scheduling. Source: WHO (30).

between: Fig. 11	 Notes and annotations for Workflow A: Registration business process
Beyond simply labelling each activity within a workflow, it is
also important to add annotations to the activities, describing,
for example, a list of forms to be filled out or other nuances
that it may not be possible to capture in a workflow diagram.
For example, if it is known that a certain activity requires 1
hour of the health worker’s time every day, that should be
recorded as an annotation. Activities that cannot be digitized
should also be labelled as such. Annotations are also a useful
way to take note of any national or global guidelines and
recommendations that might have shaped a specific workflow.
Fig. 11 provides an example of annotations from the ANC
registration workflow.
If there are any updates to the guidelines, this reference can
be a useful prompt to update the next iteration of the solution.
Noting any relevant guidelines could also serve as a reference
for any deviations from them in the workflow and could help
to highlight any roadblocks or challenges preventing health
workers from adhering to guidelines.

narrative.text: Fig. 10, 'Workflow A: Registration business process', is a BPMN-style swimlane diagram. The pool is 'Health facility', with lanes Client and Health worker or Clerk. The client arrives at the facility (1), then rapid assessment and management (2) leads to 'Urgent referral necessary?' (3); Yes ends in C. ANC referral. No leads to gather client details (4), then search for client (5) and 'Match found?' (6). No leads to create client record (7); Yes leads to a grouped subprocess 8, Validate client details: review sociodemographic data with the client (8.1), 'Update needed?' (8.2), then update client details (8.3). Both paths reach check-in client (9), ending in B. ANC contact. Fig. 11, 'Notes and annotations for Workflow A: Registration business process', is a three-column text panel that annotates each numbered activity of Fig. 10 — for example, that rapid assessment is outside the DAK's scope, and the identifiers a client may present when searched for. Both cite WHO (29).

narrative.text: Fig. 12, 'Is each and every data element collected truly needed?'. Three rows, each reading Question → Explanation → Action to be taken, with arrows chaining each row's action into the next question. 1. Is the data element duplicated? Duplicates may share a definition under different labels, or be collected on several forms; reconcile them into one element collected once. 2. Is the data element needed for service delivery or accountability? Ask whether it supports clinical decision-making, mandatory reporting or accountability; if not, consider removing it to reduce the data-entry burden on health workers. 3. Is the data element orphaned? Orphaned data is hard to use without its context; link it to its primary data elements (anything not needed will already have gone at question 2).

narrative.text: Fig. 14, 'Decision-support logic for a clinical care pathway in the form of a decision tree'. It starts at 'Antenatal registration — provider-initiated HIV testing & counselling' and splits on the result. HIV-positive leads to PMTCT, treatment, support and an offer of partner notification, then partner testing. Partner HIV-negative leads to reassessing the woman's risk and offering partner referral for VMMC. Partner not tested or HIV-positive leads to offering the partner HIV treatment (if positive), condom promotion and risk-reduction counselling. HIV-negative leads to standard post-test guidance and counselling on prevention, then two branches: offer partner testing and a risk assessment (which feeds partner testing), and a risk assessment using a tool. That tool separates a woman at substantial risk of HIV acquisition from one who is not. At substantial risk, she is offered comprehensive prevention options — STI screening and treatment, condom promotion, risk-reduction counselling, PrEP with emphasis on adherence, and follow-up ANC visits. A woman who chooses to initiate PrEP then receives clinical laboratory assessments, adherence counselling, and emphasis on follow-up visits and repeat HIV testing. Source: WHO (29).

narrative.text: Fig. 15, 'Levels of insight gained from different prototypes'. The vertical axis is level of prototype fidelity and the horizontal axis is the time required to develop the protocol. An arrow climbs through three phases: Validation, with low-fidelity prototypes (sketches, wireframes); Refinement, with moderate-fidelity prototypes (mockups); and Deployment, with higher-fidelity prototypes (clickable prototypes). Under each phase are the questions it answers. Validation asks: do users need this, and would this digital record solve their administrative reporting problems? Refinement asks: could it improve service delivery or accountability, and will users use it as intended? Deployment asks: does it have the key features, will users adopt it, and what behaviour change or roadblocks to adoption must be addressed? Adapted from Norman Tran/Stanford school (35).
